cues.en: Now with those shuffled answers
being displayed here,
it's time to make sure that once we select an answer,
we move on to the next answer in line.
And to do that, we must make sure
that this question index here changes over time
because this question index here determines
which question is our current question,
which then determines which question text
and which question answers are shown on the screen.
So how can we change this index?
Well by managing it as state again,
and that's why I created questions screen
as a stateful widget
so that we can manage and change state in there.
We should now add a new variable here
in this questions screen state class.
And that could be the current question index.
The name is up to you,
but of course it should describe which kind of value
will be stored inside of it.
Now initially this should probably be set to zero
so that we start with
the first question in our list of questions,
but it should then change
whenever we click one of these answer buttons.
Therefore, we also must add a method
to this questions screen state class here,
and that method could be called answer question
because that is what we're in the end doing
when we click one of these answer buttons,
we answer the question.
And as a result of doing that,
we wanna move on to the next question.
But of course later we also wanna make sure
that we store the answer that was picked.
So therefore here we have the answer question function,
which doesn't return anything.
And in there I want
to increase current question index by one.
Now this can be done by setting current question index
equal to current question index plus one.
This might look strange at first,
but you can access the variable,
which you then set on the left side of the equal sign,
also on the right side of the equal sign
to derive the new value to which it should be set,
because that right side will actually be executed first.
So here, when this line of code executes,
Dart will first take a look at current question index
here on the right side of the equal sign
and take the value that's currently stored in there.
Initially that will be zero.
It'll then add one to it so that overall
for the first time this function is executed,
we would have a value of one here.
And then this new value is stored back into this variable.
So that is how we can increment this variable.
And since this is something you will find yourself doing
quite often in code,
Dart actually also gives you a shortcut for this.
Instead of writing it like this, which you can do,
but which is a bit long,
you can also set current question index plus equal one.
This code is equal to this code.
By using this plus equal operator,
You are telling Dart that you wanna set this variable
equal to its current value plus one.
So this is simply a shortcut for this.
And if you want to increment the value by one,
there's an even shorter syntax
because you can then also just set
current question index plus plus.
This increments the value by one, and only by one.
So if you wanna add two to that value,
this syntax could not be used.
This syntax could be used though.
